theorems.name: Cauchy–Riemann Equations
theorems.statement: If f=u+iv is differentiable at z0, then u_x=v_y and u_y=-v_x at that point; conversely, these plus continuous partials nearby imply differentiability.
theorems.conditions: The converse direction needs continuity of the partial derivatives, not just their existence.
theorems.intuition: Differentiability requires the same derivative value approaching from the real and imaginary directions; equating those two expressions gives the equations.
theorems.proofSketch: Compute f'(z0) along h real and h purely imaginary separately, then equate real/imaginary parts.
theorems.example: f(z)=z^2 satisfies both equations everywhere and is entire.
theorems.examReady: Compute u_x,u_y,v_x,v_y; check both equations; state domain of validity.

theorems.name: Cauchy's Integral Formula
theorems.statement: f(z0) = (1/2\pi i)\oint_C f(z)/(z-z0)\,dz for f analytic on/inside simple closed contour C, z0 inside C.
theorems.conditions: f must be analytic on and inside C; z0 must be strictly inside C (0 if outside, by Cauchy's Theorem).
theorems.intuition: Boundary values of an analytic function completely determine its interior values.
theorems.proofSketch: Shrink C to a small circle around z0 using Cauchy's Theorem, then take the radius to 0.
theorems.examReady: Check z0 is inside C; if f analytic throughout, apply formula directly.
